subject: CPRA addendum: service-provider wording, subprocessor notice & onshore fallback
messages:

Subject: CPRA addendum: service provider vs processor language + subprocessor/onshore ask

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks for taking this. We're working through HealthTech's US privacy addendum (CPRA/CA) and a few open items are blocking procurement:

- We need an explicit statement that Redwood will act as a "Service Provider" under CPRA (not an Operator) — can you confirm?
- Subprocessor visibility & timing: our security team needs confirmation you will provide a subprocessor list and 30 days' notice before onboarding any new subprocessor that will access telemetry. Is that possible?
- Onshore fallback: due to regulatory needs for some of our clinical customers, we need an option for an onshore fallback for telemetry routing / log export in emergencies. Is there a mechanism or contractual language we can rely on?

Can you send a short redline or sample language we can share with our legal team? Also, please let me know if any of this requires an SLA or dedicated capacity add-on.

Cheers,
Sam

Subject: Re: CPRA addendum: service provider vs processor language + subprocessor/onshore ask

Sam — looping in our internal privacy and infra leads to make this concrete. Short answers up front: yes, we accept Service Provider/Processor (limited-use) role language in CPRA addenda with conditions; we can provide subprocessor notice and a maintained list; onshore fallback can be offered as an enterprise option tied to Dedicated/Private deployments or a documented emergency playbook for hosted customers.

Key caveats:
- Service Provider language: we'll accept a CPRA/US addendum that uses "Service Provider" terminology as long as the addendum: (a) includes a limited-use clause (no sale, no advertising, only processing for specified purposes), and (b) allows us to use subprocessors and standard cloud providers under notice/controls.
- Subprocessor notice: 30 days notice is reasonable — we typically provide a maintained CSV of subprocessors and notify customers of changes. For high-risk telemetry access (e.g., raw request payloads), we recommend an approval/objection period of 15 business days after notice.
- Onshore fallback: for Hosted customers we can document an emergency onshore routing playbook (data encryption, temporary egress, locality controls) but cannot commit to permanent onshore processing without Dedicated/Private. For enterprise commitments, Dedicated pools or Private deployments can provide an onshore fallback SLA.

Naomi (legal) — can you draft suggested CPRA wording (subprocessor notice window, objection flow, and a short onshore fallback clause) and attach a redline? Aditya/Logan — I included you to confirm the operational feasibility for telemetry routing and to attach the current subprocessor roster.

Thanks — I'll follow up with Sam once we have the redline.

Best,

Subject: Re: CPRA addendum: service provider vs processor language + subprocessor/onshore ask

Thanks Kimberly — drafting notes and proposed language below. High level: we can accept Service Provider labeling with tight limited-use commitments and a short, practical subprocessor notice / objection flow. Onshore fallback should be scoped as an optional add-on or emergency provision for hosted customers; permanent onshore processing is limited to Dedicated/Private.

Proposed CPRA addendum snippets (suggest you paste into their draft):

1) Service Provider / Limited Use
"Redwood Inference acts as a Service Provider with respect to Customer Personal Information. Redwood shall process such Personal Information only to provide the services expressly described in the Agreement and any addenda, and shall not retain, use, or disclose Personal Information for any other purpose, including for advertising or sale as defined under the CPRA."

2) Subprocessor notice & objection
"Redwood will maintain an up-to-date list of subprocessors and make it available via a secure link. Redwood shall provide Customer with at least thirty (30) days' prior notice before permitting a new subprocessor to process Personal Information that includes telemetry or other high-sensitivity data. Upon receipt of notice, Customer shall have fifteen (15) business days to object in writing to Redwood. If Customer reasonably objects based on documented security/compliance concerns, the Parties will use good faith efforts to agree on mitigation or, if no resolution is reached within thirty (30) days, Customer may require Redwood to (i) not engage the proposed subprocessor for Customer's data, or (ii) migrate affected workloads to a Dedicated/Private environment at mutually agreed commercial terms."

3) Onshore fallback (emergency and enterprise option)
"Emergency onshore fallback: For Hosted customers, Redwood shall maintain an emergency onshore routing playbook to enable temporary onshore retention or egress of telemetry in response to documented regulatory requirements or lawful orders, provided Customer has executed an addendum acknowledging associated costs and any change in service scope.

Enterprise onshore option: For Customers that procure Dedicated or Private deployments, Redwood shall provide options for onshore-only processing and storage subject to capacity, network configuration, and a separate commercial commitment."

Operational notes (for internal team):
- Subprocessor list: attach the CSV (see Kimberly's attachment). We should ensure subprocessors are annotated with region, role, and access level.
- Emergency routing: Aditya, can the infra team produce a short playbook (internal runbook + customer-facing summary) for emergency onshore egress and the manual steps required? Estimate: initial playbook in 2 weeks, validated test in 6 weeks for enterprise customers.
- Evidence: for customers asking for proof, SOC 2 + written subprocessor contracts (and optionally a signed DPA) are primary artifacts.

I'll attach a redline and a plain-text clause set for Sam. Let me know if we want stronger objection remedies.

Naomi Feldman
